blurb.text: The island of Pelops, where Mycenae rich in gold, Argos and Sparta hold their thrones.
Athena's olive-crowned peninsula — Athens of Cecrops and Theseus, and Eleusis of the Mysteries.
Boeotia and Phocis — seven-gated Thebes of Cadmus, and the Delphic seat of Apollo's oracle.
Euboea of the Abantes, the long island leaning across the narrow Euripus strait.
Iolcus of Jason and Mount Pelion of the Centaurs, where the Argo was timbered.
Dodona's oak-grove oracle, the oldest voice of Zeus among the mountains of the west.
The northern marches beneath Mount Olympus, throne of the deathless gods.
The three-fingered peninsula — Pallene of the Giants' battle, Sithonia, and Athos.
Odysseus' rocky Ithaca and the western sea-roads home from Troy.
Lemnos, where Hephaestus fell from heaven, and Samothrace of the Mysteries.
The Cyclades wheeling around holy Delos, where Leto bore Apollo and Artemis.
Minos' labyrinth-island, where infant Zeus was hidden and the bull-born Minotaur prowled.
Priam's country between Mount Ida and the Hellespont, where sacred Ilion stood and fell.
Argos, Mycenae and Tiryns — the heartland of Perseus' line and the Atreid kings.
Sparta of Menelaus and Helen, in the Eurotas valley between Taygetus and Parnon.
Sandy Pylos, where old Nestor counselled the Achaeans from his hall.
Pan's upland haunt — Lycaon's impious table and Callisto turned she-bear.
Olympia's plain, won by Pelops in the fatal chariot-race with Oenomaus.
The northern shore-strip that kept the Achaeans' name after they fled the Dorians.
Wealthy Corinth on the Isthmus — Sisyphus' Ephyra and Medea's bitter refuge.
The olive plain of Athens, prize of Athena's contest with Poseidon.
Megara between the gulfs, where Nisus' purple lock was betrayed by his own daughter.
Telamon's island kingdom, home of the greater Ajax.
Aeacus' isle, where Zeus turned ants into the Myrmidon people.
Cadmus' seven-gated Thebes and Mount Helicon, where the Muses taught Hesiod song.
Delphi under Parnassus, where Apollo slew the Python and took the oracle.
Opus of Patroclus' boyhood, before the killing that sent him to Phthia.
The western Locrians above Naupactus, where the Heraclids built their ships.
Aegimius' little Doris, whose king Heracles defended against the Lapiths.
Trachis and Mount Oeta, where Heracles mounted his own pyre.
Calydon of Oeneus, where Meleager led the hunt for the great boar.
West of the Achelous, named for Acarnan, Alcmaeon's son.
Old country of the Lapiths, who fought the Centaurs at Pirithous' wedding.
Pelasgian Argos and Larissa of the horse-plains.
Pelion of Chiron the centaur, above Iolcus where the Argo was timbered.
The southwest plain of the Enipeus, the river-god Tyro loved.
Achilles' Phthia, mustering-ground of the Myrmidons.
The wild northern coast of Epirus — where Helenus built Buthrotum, the little Troy of the Trojan seer.
Dodona's oak oracle and the kingdom Neoptolemus founded after Troy.
Thesprotia of the Acheron — where Cichyrus stood near the lake Acherusia and the rivers Cocytus and Acheron, which Pausanias believed Homer had seen before he described the regions of Hades.

Ambracia on the Ambracian gulf — the Epirote city Aeneas passed on his westward voyage, disputed in myth between the gods, and where Hyginus says the bones of Neoptolemus were scattered after Orestes slew him at Delphi.
The high cantons under the Pindus, springs of the Haliacmon.
Pieria beneath Olympus' north face, birthplace of the Muses.
Emathia of Pierus, whose nine daughters dared the Muses to song.
The Paeonians of the broad Axios, Troy's far-northern allies.
The lake country toward the Strymon, whose river-god fathered Rhesus.
Thrace of Boreas and bloody Ares, where Orpheus sang to the trees.
Golden Thasos, settled by the Phoenician kin of Cadmus.
Samothrace of the great Mysteries, Poseidon's watchtower over the war at Troy.
The mainland base of the trident peninsula.
Pallene, where the gods and Giants joined battle.
The middle finger of the trident, between holy capes.
The easternmost finger, crowned by Mount Athos.
Drepane of the Phaeacians, where Jason wed Medea and Odysseus washed ashore.
The white Leucadian rock the dead pass on their way below.
Same of the Cephallenians, who sailed under Odysseus' command.
Rocky Ithaca, Odysseus' hard-won home.
Wooded Zacynthus of the suitors' roll-call.
Dulichium — where Phyleus made his home in wrath against his father, and whence Meges led forty ships to Troy.
Lesbos, prize of Achilles' raids, where Orpheus' singing head came ashore.
Lemnos, where Hephaestus fell from heaven and the Argonauts met Hypsipyle.
Chios of king Oenopion, who blinded the hunter Orion.
Samos, island of Hera's great sanctuary.
Icaria, where the sea took falling Icarus and kept his name.
The Sporades — scattered isles off Magnesia and Euboea, where the Argo passed Sciathus and Peparethos on the outward voyage.
Scyros of Lycomedes — where Thetis hid Achilles in maiden's dress, where Neoptolemus was born, and where Theseus met his end.
Sciathus — the westernmost of the Northern Sporades, sighted from the Argo as Jason's crew sailed past Pelion toward Magnesia.
Peparethos, rich in olives — the Sporades isle that gave its name to Peparethus, son of Dionysus and Ariadne, and that Minos passed seeking Aeacus.
Ikos, the easternmost of the Northern Sporades off the Magnesian coast — in the same island chain as Sciathus and Peparethos on the Argonaut route.
Holy Delos, the floating island that anchored for Leto's twins.
Naxos, where Theseus left Ariadne and Dionysus found her.
Paros of Minos' sons, raided by Heracles on his Amazon voyage.
Melos of the Cyclades — where Menestheus son of Peteos reigned after King Polyanax died on the homeward voyage from Troy.
Level Myconos of the Cyclades — where Thetis buried the Locrian Ajax after Athena wrecked his ship on the voyage home from Troy, and one of the isles that sided with Minos against Athens.
Andros of the northern Cyclades — where Phidippus son of Thessalus settled with the Coans after Troy, before the wind drove them on to Cyprus.
Sea-girt Tenos — where Heracles slew the winged Boreads Zetes and Calais, and where Athena later sent a tempest against the Greek fleet sailing home from Troy.

Ceos of the western Cyclades — where Aristaeus son of Apollo made his home after Sirius scorched the Minoan isles, built the altar of Zeus Icmaeus, and ended the plague with sacrifices on the mountains.
Kimolos of the western Cyclades — the chalky island whose fields joined Minos' allies when he mustered the Cyclades against the Athenians.
Level Seriphos — where Danae and the infant Perseus washed ashore in a chest, Dictys the fisherman reared the hero, and King Polydectes was turned to stone by the Gorgon's head.
Siphnos of the gold mines — whose tithe built the treasury at Delphi until greed stopped the offering and the sea swallowed the workings, and home of Arne the impious Siphnian turned to a daw.
Syros covered with wild thyme — one of the Cycladic isles that sided with Minos when he gathered the islands against Athens.
Calliste-Thera, sprung from the clod Euphemus let fall into the sea.
Rhodes of the nymph Rhodos, beloved island of Helios.
Cos, where storm-driven Heracles came ashore and fought the Meropes.
Holy Cythera, where Aphrodite first came ashore from the sea-foam.
Cyprus of Aphrodite — Kypris' island, where Teucer founded a second Salamis after Troy.
The Ionian coast of Asia Minor — Miletus, Ephesus and the cities that looked across the Aegean to Greece.
The kingdom at the eastern Black Sea — Aea of Aeetes, where the Golden Fleece hung and Jason's Argonauts won Medea.
The golden kingdom of Croesus — Sardis on Tmolus, where Midas washed away his touch and Omphale held Heracles in servitude.
The Carian coast — Halicarnassus of Mausolus and Artemisia, and the isles the Carians held with Miletus.
The southern Black Sea coast — Sinope where Zeus gave the nymph her name and her virginity.
The Caicus plain — Teuthrania of old, where Telephus ruled and the Greeks first ravaged the shore thinking it Troy.
Phrygia by the Sangarius — Gordius and Midas, Marsyas' contest, and the golden touch washed away on Tmolus.
Lycia of the eddying Xanthus — Sarpedon and Glaucus led its men to Troy, and Bellerophon fought the Solymi in the hills above.
Pamphylia on the southern coast — where Cretan settlers dwelt beside Lycians and Carians, kin to Sarpedon's line.
Cilicia of Thebe under Placus — Eëtion's kingdom, father of Andromache whom bronze-harnessed Hector wed.
Bithynia on the Propontis shore — where King Amycus, son of a Bithynian nymph, forced strangers to box and die.
Paphlagonia of the Eneti — Pylaemenes led them from Cytorus and Sesamus to fight beside the Trojans.
Cappadocia on the Euxine rim — where the Tauric goddess' fame still reached, and Artemis Anaeitis was claimed.
Dardania about Mount Ida — Aeneas son of Anchises led the Dardanians, whom Aphrodite bore to a mortal amid the spurs of Ida.
Teuthrania on the Mysian coast — where Telephus ruled after Teuthras wed Auge, and old Pergamus took its name.
Aeolis of the twelve cities — Hesiod's Aeolian Cyme and the coast the Ionians later disputed at Panionium.
Maeonia beneath Tmolus — the older name of Lydia's heartland, whence Mesthles and Antiphus led the Maeonians to Troy.
Ascania in Phrygia — Phorcys and Ascanius led the Phrygian host from afar to the plain of Troy.
Hellespontine Phrygia — the Dardanian shore where Telephus' kingdom touched the straits and the Sangarius ran inland.
Trinacria of the three capes — where Polyphemus kept his Cyclopes cave, Scylla lurked in the strait, Arethusa sought refuge, and Etna still breathes fire from the buried battle of the gods.
Great Greece on Italian soil — Achaean Tarentum and Ionian Croton, Sybaris and Locri, where colonists built temples to the gods they brought from Hellas.
Latium of the Laurentine shore — where Aeneas came ashore after Troy and won his place among the Latin peoples.
Liguria on the Eridanus — where King Cycnus left his peopled cities to mourn Phaethon among the Heliades' poplars and was changed into a swan.
Campania's western plain — where Philoctetes settled among the Campanians after Troy, and where Diomedes wandered in the same nostoi strand toward Cumae.
Sardinia at the western horizon — the island where Pausanias sends Aristaeus after Actaeon's death and where early Greek colonists from Iolaus and Theras crossed the sea.
Libya beyond the Greek map — the western land where Atlas holds up heaven and where Guneus son of Ocytus settled by the Cinyps after Troy.
Aethiopia at the southern horizon — the kingdom of Cepheus where Cassiopeia's boast against the Nereids chained Andromeda to the rock and Perseus turned Cetus to stone.
Egypt beyond the Greek map — where Io ended her wanderings as a cow, Danaus fled the sons of Aegyptus, and Menelaus was storm-driven for eight years until he bound Proteus on Pharos.
Mesopotamia at the eastern horizon — Semiramis' brick Babylon where Pyramus and Thisbe whispered through the party wall, and where Ninus' tomb stood outside the city gate.
Phoenicia on the Syrian coast — Agenor's kingdom when Zeus bore Europa away in bull-form, and the homeland his sons Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix were forbidden to return to without her.
Illyria of the Encheleans — where Cadmus and Harmonia ended their exile, led the tribe against the Illyrians, and were at last turned to crested serpents.
Tauris of the Taurians — the Scythian shore where Artemis made Iphigenia priestess and where Orestes came to steal the image from the bloody altar.
